source: Bouzenia and Pradel (2025) Understanding Software Engineering Agents: A Study of Thought-Action-Result Trajectories
finding: Closest LLM analogue to Ko and Uttl clustering. They parsed agent logs into thought-action-result steps and compared successful and failed runs by action n-grams. Successful runs balance exploring, explaining and validating. Failed runs repeat the same actions without adapting.
numbers: 120 trajectories (40 each from RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover, OpenHands), 2,822 iterations. Mean length: RepairAgent 34, OpenHands 29, AutoCodeRover 6. RepairAgent failed runs 40 steps vs 22 for successful. Thought-action misalignment: OpenHands 0.5% in successful vs 1.4% in failed runs; AutoCodeRover 0% vs 4.8%. Three anti-patterns: repeated identical actions without follow-up, consecutive fix generation without testing, stopping without validated tests.
limits: Descriptive. Three agents with different built-in procedures, so agent identity is confounded with behaviour. Only 40 runs per agent, success label from original evaluation. No clustering into named strategies, no control for task difficulty (hard tasks give longer runs). Not a causal test of strategy.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: behavioural motifs do separate success from failure, but this is difficulty and procedure confounded. Anti-pattern checks (no repeated fixes without testing, no stopping without validation) are cheap guardrail candidates.

source: Chen et al. (2025/2026) SWE-Exp: Experience-Driven Software Issue Resolution
finding: Retrieved distilled experience (a bug-class lesson from past issues in other repositories) raises resolve rate with the model fixed. Abstracting the experience matters more than raw examples.
numbers: SWE-Bench Verified, 500 issues, Pass@1. DeepSeek-V3-0324: 42.0% with SWE-Exp vs 35.4-38.8% for agent baselines. Claude 4 Sonnet: 73.0% vs baselines 66.6-71.6%. Ablations on DeepSeek-V3: no comprehension experience 38.8; no modification experience 39.4; no experience extraction (raw problem plus gold patch as demo) 36.0 (-6.0); similarity instead of LLM reranking 38.2. Leakage control: same-repository and later experiences excluded. Zero experiences 37.8 vs one 42.0.
limits: Experience bank is built from the same benchmark's other issues (cross-repo, time-ordered). Ablations on a single weaker model only, one run each, no confidence intervals. Baseline rows in the extracted table are jumbled, so baseline numbers are given as ranges. Not equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a good retrieved lesson gives about +4 points (37.8 to 42.0) on a mid model, about +3 on a strong model. Raw demonstrations add little over none; abstraction is the useful part. Supports a lesson store keyed by bug class, one lesson at a time.

source: Chen et al. (2025/2026) SWE-Exp: effect of more or conflicting experiences
finding: More retrieved experience made results worse, and forcing the agent to cite experience made it keep using it after the environment showed otherwise. This is the nearest measured cost of misleading retrieved knowledge.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3, SWE-Bench Verified: 0 experiences 37.8%, 1 experience 42.0%, 2 experiences 39.8%, 4 experiences 39.0%. The text gives the baseline once as 37.2% and once as 37.8%. Letting the instructor explicitly cite comprehension experiences was worse than passing experience as plain context.
quote: too much dependence: the Instructor continued using experience even after enough environment exploration
limits: Not a controlled wrong-fact injection. 'Misleading' here means irrelevant or conflicting retrieved lessons, not deliberately false facts. Single model, single run, no CIs.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: retrieval has a sweet spot at one item. A lesson should be advisory context, never a forced step. Add a rule to drop a lesson when fresh evidence contradicts it.

source: Liang, Garg and Moghaddam (2025) The SWE-Bench Illusion: When State-of-the-Art LLMs Remember Instead of Reason
finding: Models can name the buggy file from the issue text alone, far more often on SWE-Bench Verified than on tasks from other repositories. So part of the benchmark score is repo-specific knowledge, not procedure. This is the LLM version of Ko and Uttl's 'bug-specific knowledge predicts success', and it is a contamination warning.
numbers: File-path identification from issue text only, no repository access: up to 76% on SWE-Bench Verified (range 60-76%), 57-71% on Full-SWE-Bench, 50-68% on newly collected SWE-Repo tasks, below 53% on tasks from repositories outside the benchmark. Five-gram overlap when reproducing the ground-truth function: up to 35% on Verified and Full vs up to 18% on other benchmarks.
limits: Diagnostic, not a causal test of knowledge on resolve rate. Memorisation and familiarity with popular repositories are mixed. Models tested are 2024-2025 frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and gap 2: familiarity (here, seen repositories) lifts localisation sharply, so any strategy comparison on SWE-bench Verified is confounded by knowledge. Use leak-filtered or fresh items. Strategy effects should be tested on rare or new repositories.

source: Deng et al. (2025) SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?
finding: On a contamination-resistant, harder benchmark the same SWE-Agent scaffold gives under 45% for all models. The fixed Agentless route was tried and dropped because it could not edit several files. Supplying requirements and interface raised pass rate roughly threefold, a large information effect.
numbers: Public set N=731: Claude Sonnet 4.5 43.6%, Sonnet 4 42.7%, GPT-5 (high) 41.8%, Haiku 4.5 39.5%, Kimi K2 27.7%, GPT-OSS-120B 16.2%. Commercial set N=276: best under 20%. Information ablation: GPT-5 25.9% with problem plus requirements plus interface vs 8.4% problem only; Opus 4.1 22.7% vs 8.2%. LLM-judge failure clusters (last 20 turns, unresolved runs): Opus 4.1 wrong solution 35.9%, syntax error 24.2%; Sonnet 4 context overflow 35.6%, endless file reading 17.0%; Qwen3-32B tool errors 42.0%.
limits: Agentless result is one sentence with no number. The information ablation partly reflects that unit tests demand specific APIs (false negatives), not only help. Failure clusters rely on a GPT-5 judge validated at 87% agreement in earlier work, not here.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and gap 3: a scripted locate-then-fix route does not survive multi-file tasks. LLM-judged failure clusters exist but cluster by failure, not by strategy. Interface and requirement information moves results much more than procedure.

source: Lam et al. (2025) CodeCrash: Exposing LLM Fragility to Misleading Natural Language in Code Reasoning (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Misleading comments and print messages pull LLMs away from the code's real behaviour, as misleading comments pulled human debuggers. A plausible wrong hint is worse than an obviously wrong comment for reasoning models.
numbers: 1,279 questions from CruxEval and LiveCodeBench, 17 LLMs plus 3 reasoning models, output prediction. Average pass@1 drop 23.2% (relative). Misleading comments (MCC) and misleading prints (MPS) each about 24% average relative drop. With chain of thought still 13.8% average drop. Comment density sweep: every model degrades as injection probability goes from 0 to 1, small models faster. Reasoning models used 2-3 times more tokens under plausible wrong hints.
limits: Task is code output prediction, not debugging or repair. Hints are GPT-4o generated and checked by hand. Temperature 0.2, one CoT sample. Does not test whether a bug fix is sent to the commented site.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 mostly closed: yes, models are steered by misleading comments, and reasoning models burn tokens trying to reconcile them. Still open: first-edit location in repair tasks.

source: Lam et al. (2025) CodeCrash: defences (ignore-comments prompt and refactoring pre-pass)
finding: A plain guardrail 'ignore the comments' does nothing under direct inference and only partly helps with chain of thought. A refactor-first pass that deletes misleading comments made MCC worse. So a prompt rule alone is not a reliable guardrail against misleading cues.
numbers: Table 8, pass@1: GPT-4o direct vanilla 64.5, with misleading comments 45.7, with ignore instruction 45.9. DeepSeek-V3 CoT: vanilla 92.1, MCC 70.2, MCC plus ignore 82.1. GPT-4o CoT: 94.4, 87.5, 89.4. Qwen2.5-72B direct MCC 48.0 vs 48.0 with ignore. Refactoring pre-pass with GPT-4o: MCC 45.7 without vs 41.1 with.
limits: Output prediction only. Single dataset mix, one prompt wording tried.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a verbal guardrail ('verify before trusting comments') is weak. A guardrail needs an action: run the code or check against output before relying on a comment. Test that arm, not the wording.

source: Meng et al. (2024/2025) An Empirical Study on LLM-based Agents for Automated Bug Fixing
finding: Six top SWE-bench Verified systems solve largely the same issues, and file-level localisation accuracy ranks the systems in nearly the same order as resolve rate. Issue text quality (stack trace, reproduction code, a suggested solution) predicts which issues get solved.
numbers: 404 of 500 solved by at least one system, 181 by all six, 96 by none. File localisation: best system hit at least one buggy file in 448 cases vs 342 for the lowest (31.0% more); all files in 394 cases. Rank order by F1 matches resolve rank except Learn-by-interact. Related reproduction scripts: 384 of 500 (76.8%); 80.4% when the issue has runnable reproduction code vs 64% when the issue has not enough information.
limits: Localisation read from final patches, not intermediate steps. Systems differ in model and scaffold, so the localisation-resolve link is correlational. Python only, 2024 systems.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: supports 'information first' (localisation) over 'procedure'. Reproduction quality depends on the issue text, which is information again.

source: Fan et al. (2025) SWE-Effi: Re-Evaluating Software AI Agent System Effectiveness Under Resource Constraints
finding: Procedure-based scaffolds and agentic scaffolds were crossed with base models under a token or cost budget. Model-scaffold fit mattered more than scaffold type. Failed runs burn far more tokens than solved runs.
numbers: 50 random SWE-bench Verified issues, 5 scaffolds (AutoCodeRover, Agentless, Agentless-Mini = procedure; OpenHands, SWE-Agent = agentic), several models. SWE-Agent: 28% resolve with Qwen3-32B (35.5 calls, 440k input tokens) vs 10% with GPT-4o-mini (181 calls, 8.1M tokens). OpenHands 34% vs 11.9%. AutoCodeRover Qwen3-32B 38% with 14.7 calls; with GPT-4o-mini 12%, above OpenHands and SWE-Agent on that model. Agentless 48% with Qwen3-32B at 83.1 calls. SWE-Agent API budget fixed at $1 per issue.
limits: Only 50 issues, so wide intervals, no CIs in the text I read. Older models (Qwen3-32B, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B). Not leak-filtered. Different scaffolds have different default limits, so tokens are not equal across arms.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 9: closest equal-budget scaffold-by-model comparison found, but it crosses scaffold with model, not with information. 'Expensive failures' (stuck runs use many more tokens) supports an early stop-and-rediagnose trigger, but no arm tests it.

source: Sun and Hansen (2026) BC-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Engineering in a Domain-Specific Language for ERP
finding: First rare-language test I found with a harness-versus-model contrast. On AL (Dynamics 365 Business Central DSL), between-model differences were larger than between-harness differences, and gains on general benchmarks did not transfer.
numbers: 101 manually curated bug-fixing tasks, five runs per task. Claude Code vs GitHub Copilot, same model: opus-4.5 57.4% vs 58.4% (p=0.728); opus-4.6 68.5% vs 65.1% (p=0.075). Model change within Copilot: opus-4.6 65.1% vs opus-4.5 59.8% (p=0.026); gpt-5.2-codex 60.8% vs gpt-5.1-codex-max 53.7% (p=0.019). GPT-4.1 16.6%. GPT-5.3-codex 55.8% below GPT-5.2-codex 60.8% despite gains on SWE-Bench Pro. Failures for Copilot with opus-4.6 (176 of 505 trials): wrong solution 44.3%, incorrect file 29.5%, incorrect region 18.2%, build failure 5.7%. AL compiler MCP and LSP tools were planned, not yet tested.
limits: Only four matched comparisons; the paper says so. Harnesses are commercial products with unknown differences, not clean strategy arms. No common-language control on the same models, so 'rare language' is inferred. Benchmark version differs between rows.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: in a rare language the model matters more than harness and finding the right place (48% of failures) dominates. Does not show the strategy effect growing or shrinking with familiarity.

source: Rashid et al. (2025) SWE-PolyBench: A multi-language benchmark for repository-level evaluation of coding agents
finding: Same model (Sonnet 3.5) with three agent designs across four languages. Python is highest for every agent. A fixed pipeline's edge was Python-only because its localisation tools were Python-specific.
numbers: 2,110 instances: Java 165, JavaScript 1,017, TypeScript 729, Python 199. Pass rate on Sonnet 3.5, Python 20-24%, Java 11-16%, TypeScript 5-13%. Overall (table order, extraction jumbled): Agentless-PB 7.8%, SWE-Agent-PB 10.2%, Aider-PB 14.1%. Aider-PB used 19-20% of the input tokens of the others. Agentless-PB led Python file and node retrieval only.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction, so the per-agent assignment of overall rates follows row order and the paper's text that Aider-PB is best. Agentless adapted (PB) by the authors, not the original. Language familiarity is confounded with repository complexity (authors note Java is more complex yet beats TypeScript).
agent_relevance: Gap 4: performance falls in less-common languages, and the scripted route's advantage depends on language-specific tools. The paper itself attributes the pattern to pretraining data distribution. No clean strategy-by-familiarity interaction.

source: Martinez and Franch (2026) Dissecting the SWE-Bench Leaderboards: Profiling Submitters and Architectures of LLM- and Agent-Based Repair Systems
finding: Across all leaderboard entries, fixed human-designed workflows no longer clearly beat autonomous single agents once base models improved. On Verified the best fixed multi-agent workflow and the best free single agent are within about 2 points.
numbers: Lite 79 entries, Verified 99 entries, 80 unique approaches. Verified: top entry 75.2% (fixed workflow, multiple agents, 5 entries); fully autonomous single-agent group up to 73.2% (31 entries, median second). Kruskal-Wallis on Verified H=19.41, p=0.0070; Dunn: fixed workflow with no agent differs from three other groups (p=0.0207, 0.0125, 0.0003). On Lite no group difference (H=12.18, p=0.0579); best Lite 60.3%.
limits: Observational leaderboard data. Entries differ in model, spend and cherry-picked runs. No leak filtering. The authors suggest better base models reduce the need for explicit scaffolding but did not test it.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 mostly closed for 2025: with strong models, scripted routes do not beat free agents; the purely fixed no-agent pipelines are worst. The fixed-route advantage seen with older models (Agentless 2024) has faded.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement (ICLR 2025)
finding: Adding search with backtracking (a rediagnose mechanism) on top of a base agent raised resolve rate for all five models. Merely letting the agent move freely between states added almost nothing.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, resolve rate, base Moatless-Adapted vs SWE-Search: GPT-4o 25.7 to 31.0; GPT-4o-mini 13.0 to 17.0; Qwen-2.5-72B 18.0 to 24.7; DeepSeek-V2.5 16.3 to 21.0; Llama-3.1-70B 13.6 to 17.7; mean +23% relative. Free state transitions alone: 24.3 (Moatless v0.0.2) to 25.7, +1.4%. Up to 100 iterations, 3 expansions per node.
limits: SWE-Search uses many more model calls than the baseline, so this is not equal tokens. Lite, older models, one run each. The gain bundles value-agent feedback, debate and backtracking.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: structured backtracking helps but costs compute; free flexibility alone invites loops. Still missing: a test of a cheap stop-and-rediagnose trigger at equal tokens.

source: Wang et al. (2024/2025) CodeRAG-Bench: Can Retrieval Augment Code Generation?
finding: Retrieved documents help most where the model knows least (rare libraries) and with strong models; retrieval quality is the limit. Weak or mismatched generators can be hurt by extra context.
numbers: Gold documents: GPT-4o +27.4 points on SWE-Bench; repo-level gains 7.5-17.2 points on RepoEval. ODEX-hard (20 least-used libraries): retrieved documents improve results by 20.3-40.1% (as written in the paper). SWE-bench with best retrieve-and-rerank plus GPT-4o: +21 points over no retrieval, still 9 points under gold. RAG did not help DeepSeekCoder on MBPP, which the paper traces to over-complicated, repetitive outputs with added context.
limits: Mostly code generation, not debugging. Gold-vs-retrieved gap is the nearest to a 'wrong fact' cost; no deliberate misleading document test. Table extraction was garbled, so I use the text claims.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 5: supports the Ko and Uttl hypothesis in reverse. Knowledge from retrieval matters most for unfamiliar libraries, so a rare-domain run should show a larger information effect than strategy effect.

source: Mundler et al. (2024) SWT-Bench: Testing and Validating Real-World Bug-Fixes with Code Agents
finding: Self-generated issue-reproducing tests are a strong filter for proposed fixes. Code agents built for repair generate such tests better than test-generation systems. Reproducing an issue and fixing it are different skills per issue.
numbers: SWE-Agent precision more than doubled on fixes that pass its own tests that failed before the fix. Ideal ensemble of the best four methods solves 71% more samples than the best single one. Correlation between repair and test generation holds overall but not per sample.
limits: The filter acts after the patch exists. It is not the same as forcing the agent to inspect output before its first edit. I did not extract the exact precision pair.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (indirect): execution evidence is valuable as a verifier. No study found that forces output inspection before the first edit for silent bugs.

source: Semantic Scholar citation graph of Ko and Uttl (2003), DOI 10.1109/WPC.2003.1199201
finding: Forward-citation check done. 56 citing papers listed. None is a replication, and none is an LLM study that tests the strategy-versus-knowledge claim. Citing work is on programming expertise, eye tracking, personality, comprehension confounders and end-user debugging.
numbers: 56 citations. Examples: Ko and Myers (2003, 2005) programming error models; Baltes and Diehl (2018) Towards a theory of software development expertise; Wiedenbeck-lineage work on non-programmers identifying functionality (2009); Automatically generated patches as debugging aids (2014); Code Comprehension Confounders: intelligence and personality (2021); 2023 attention networks on debugging; 2026 RLV vulnerability detection (tangential).
limits: Semantic Scholar coverage is incomplete (Google Scholar would list more). Titles only; I did not open the citing papers. The Ko and Uttl paper is in a workshop proceedings and cited mostly as background.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 closed for what is indexable: no direct replication exists in the indexed record. The headline stays single-source. Do not claim support from citing work.

source: Absence check for a 2x2 of strategy by information at equal tokens on one model (gap 1)
finding: I found no 2024-2026 paper that crosses fixed versus free procedure with execution feedback or retrieved knowledge on versus off at equal tokens on one model. The nearest are SWE-Effi (scaffold by model), BC-Bench (model versus harness), SWE-Exp (experience on versus off, strategy fixed) and SWT-Bench (tests as filter).
numbers: No study located. Closest equal-budget design: SWE-Effi 5 scaffolds, 50 issues. Closest information on/off: SWE-Exp 37.8 vs 42.0 (DeepSeek-V3, Verified); SWE-Bench Pro 25.9 vs 8.4 with requirements on/off (GPT-5).
limits: Absence of evidence. The web search quota ran out during this pass; I used Semantic Scholar, arXiv pages and direct paper PDFs only, and Semantic Scholar rate-limited many queries. Searches for trajectory-clustering and workflow-versus-agent studies returned nothing usable, which is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. Run the 2x2 on our own items.
